abstract: With computer-assisted proofs that $\mathbb{C}^6$ admits at most three mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) now available, $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is the smallest dimension in which it is unknown whether a complete set of $d+1=11$ MUBs exists; only three MUBs are known. We prove that every triple of mutually unbiased product bases of $\mathbb{C}^2\otimes\mathbb{C}^5$ is strongly unextendible: no vector is unbiased to all three bases. Consequently no set of four MUBs in dimension ten, and in particular no complete set, contains three product bases. This settles the case $d=2\times5$ anticipated by McNulty, Pammer and Weigert; it was known only for the Heisenberg-Weyl triple. The proof covers all ten equivalence classes with explicit Nullstellensatz certificates modulo one prime on $91$ charts of $\mathbb{P}^9\times\mathbb{P}^9$ for each class ($910$ in all), transferred to characteristic zero by a projective reduction lemma, together with an independent rank certificate for eight of the ten classes. We also prove that the pair formed by the standard and the Fourier basis of $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is contained in no set of four MUBs. Exactly $3040$ rays are unbiased to both bases (this confirms the count found numerically by Führ and Rzeszotnik), each of them is unbiased to at most eight of the others, and every triple formed by the pair and a third MUB is strongly unextendible. For this we certify $34,940$ cyclic $10$-roots in Krawczyk uniqueness boxes, decide unimodularity exactly through an involution, and prove completeness by a four-dimensional interval branch-and-bound obtained from the Chinese-remainder splitting $\mathbb{Z}_{10}=\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$.
